title: Chapter 142 – Waking the Head
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The stair is warm, and Jian knows whose warmth it is.

He stands at the top of it in the cold gray before dawn, with a lamp in one hand and Lu Fei's chalk-white face at his shoulder, and he puts the flat of his palm against the first step. It is like touching the side of a sleeping animal. The stone is not hot. It is the heat of a body that has been held in someone's arms all night. Under it, faint and slow, a pulse is going.

"It has not changed since the burial," Lu Fei whispers. "Not a degree. Head Wuping thinks it is a good sign."

"It is a good sign."

"You do not sound as if you think so."

"I think it is a loan." He lifts his hand. "Ye did not stop at the thirteenth name. She gave the Gate the last thing she had."

Lu Fei says nothing. She is a clever woman. She works it out in the time it takes the lamp to gutter, and her lips part and shut again.

Ye said one word as she died. Remain. It is the fourth word in the Founders' first sentence, the hooked one, the word that tells a thing to stay where it is. Jian heard it from Pei Wanli, who was kneeling at her feet and has not stopped repeating it since. He did not understand it then. He understands it now. A hundred and twenty-four years of name, spoken into a Gate that has gone hungry for six hundred, is not nothing. It is a meal. It has bought the Chain a season, perhaps two.

It has bought him time. She meant it to. She sat in the dark with her failing eye and planned her own death like a lesson, and he thinks that if he were not the Keeper of anything he would sit down on this stair and weep.

Instead he says, "Show me the number again."

She unrolls the reading. The ragged peaks of the Gate wall have settled into a clean, shallow wave. Under it, in her small neat hand, she has written a figure and underlined it twice.

Nine weeks.

"Perhaps ten," she says. "After that I do not know."

"Midwinter is in six."

"Yes."

"Then I have three weeks to learn how to do a thing I have not done." He takes the lamp. "Wait here. If I am not up by sunset, tell Wuping to ring the bell."

* * *

He has been planning it for seven months.

It began in the Orchard, with the tape, and a single sentence from Ethan Cole's tired voice. The Chain was never meant to hold them. It was meant to be held. A chain that holds nobody is a rope tied to nothing. It is a name, written and left to dry. Jian lay awake for a month turning that over, and in the third week he understood what Sang Ruo had known and could not say.

The sleepers are not fuel. They are entries.

Thirty-one men and women, each lying on a jade slab in the ridge-house, each with a thread-knot at the skull. The Second House says the thread feeds the Gate, and that is true, but it is the second truth. The first is older. The Roll of Keepers, which Sang Ruo carried and Ye guarded and the Warden now covets, was never a list of dead officials. It is a ledger of debts. Every Keeper who ever sat the Seat took a sleeper into his keeping, and the sleeper's name went on the Roll in the Keeper's hand. And a name on the Roll can be read.

That is what Ye proved, in twenty-four years. A name that has been burned can be read home. A name that has been kept can be read out.

He has never been sure it would work on the sleepers. He has been sure it would cost.

The seven-hundred-and-first step is the last. Below it the Dock opens, a vast dim round room of black stone and cold light, with the Gate wall standing at the far end of it like a closed eye. He has been here four times in two years. It has never frightened him. Today it feels crowded, as if there were people in the walls.

He sets the lamp on the floor. He kneels.

```

He reads the panel twice. It is the plainest warning the interface has ever given him. Not reversible. In all these years it has never used that word.

He does not confirm. He thinks about the cost.

One hundred and ten of the Reservoir's banked one hundred and eighty-six. That is fifteen years of his own labor, and the bulk of it was meant for Wenyuan's next step. Seal, perhaps ten points, perhaps more. And "memory-index write," which in the interface's flat language means that something he carries will be taken to pay for the rest, and he will not be allowed to choose.

It always costs, he thinks. That is how I know it is the right thing.

He puts his hand on the cold floor.

"Confirm."

* * *

He reads them as Sang Ruo taught him, in the old script, at the pace of a man walking up a hill.

He has the names. They were given to him in the Quiet Seat, ten years ago, by the sleepers themselves, in a hurried whisper that he copied in a notebook. Thirty-one. Seven on the page are crossed through in Ye's red ink: seven graves under the ridge, and he reads those too, because a name does not stop mattering when its owner does.

"Chen Boyuan," he says. "Who kept the Seventh Gate. Who loved sour plums. Who gave his sleep to the House at thirty-eight, to pay a brother's debt. You are home."

The Dock is silent.

"Su Linfeng. Who could not read. Who counted by knots. You are home."

The Gate wall does not stir. He reads on. Each name is a stone he sets on the stone before it, and by the ninth he finds that his voice has gone flat and steady, as Ye's did. By the twelfth, his throat burns. By the sixteenth the lamp has begun to gutter and the vast room is filling, very faintly, with a pale light that comes from nowhere, from the walls, from the air itself, a light like the inside of a pearl.

He ignores it. He reads the seventeenth. The eighteenth. At the twenty-second his hands are shaking so hard he has to press them flat on the floor, and at the twenty-fifth something warm runs down his upper lip and he tastes iron. Blood. He does not wipe it. If he stops, he thinks, he will not start again.

"Yan Rongzhi," he says, at the thirtieth.

The light in the Dock changes.

It does not brighten. It deepens, as though someone has opened a door onto a larger room. The pearl-colored glow draws in and gathers into a single point above the Gate wall, a bead of gold the size of a seed, hanging in the air, trembling. Jian feels it on his skin like a held breath.

"Who was Head of the Azure Cloud Sect for sixty-three years," he says. "Who walked into the Founders' Chamber on his own feet, and lay down on the slab, and asked the House to take his sleep so that the Gate would not take a child's. Who has not seen the sun in seventy years. Who is afraid, and went anyway." His voice cracks. "Yan Rongzhi. You are home."

The gold seed flares.

For a moment the whole Dock is a single blaze of light. Then it is dark. Complete, soft, ringing dark, and in the dark, from far above, far up the seven hundred and one steps, comes the sound of someone drawing a long, shuddering, ragged breath.

Then another voice.

Then a dozen.

* * *

They wake all at once, and they wake screaming.

It is not a cry of pain. It is the cry of a drowning swimmer breaking the surface, and he hears it through two miles of rock, rising from the ridge-house like a storm: twenty-four voices, old and young, men and women, calling out names he does not know. Mothers. Brothers. Gods. Somebody is laughing in a high cracked giggle that goes on and on.

He is on his hands and knees. He can hear his own heart. There is blood on the floor under his chin, a spreading black coin of it, and when he tries to stand the Dock tilts under him like a deck.

```
READING 31/31 :: COMPLETE
DRAW: 112 CE (Reservoir 186 -> 74)
SEAL: 54% (-9)
ROLL: "Lin Jian" written. 32nd Keeper. Entry CLOSED.
MEMORY-INDEX WRITE: 1 item removed.
[REDACTED: voice / Elder Ye / age 100+]
COLE DOOR :: PAGE 2 LOCKED (Seal < 60%)
```

He stares at it. He reads it again.

Voice. Elder Ye.

He tries to remember the sound of her. He can see her. The dry, high forehead. The black stick. The one good eye. He can hear what she said: You look like a candle. The words are there. But the voice that said them is not. There is a flat gray space where it was, smooth as a polished stone, and no matter how he feels along its edges he can find no seam.

He has lost Kuang's laugh, and Bai's voice, and now this. He had thought he was prepared. It turns out that grief is something you cannot prepare for in the abstract. It must be paid in the particular.

He sits with it for a long moment, on the black floor, in the dark. Then he wipes the blood from his mouth with the heel of his hand and gets to his feet.

Page 2 is locked, he thinks. The door I have been walking toward for years has closed because I spent nine points of Seal on thirty-one strangers.

He does not feel as bad as he expected.

* * *

The ridge-house is chaos when he climbs into it, and for the first time in years he is glad of it.

It is a long low hall with a gabled roof, cold and bare, and thirty-one jade slabs set in rows on the floor like beds in a field hospital. Twenty-four of them are occupied. On each a person lies or sits or sprawls: pale, emaciated, white-haired, blinking at the roof beams with the terrible bewildered attention of the newly born. Pupils and servants run between them with blankets and water jugs and bowls of rice gruel. Lu Fei has fetched half the Pill Hall. Somewhere a woman is shouting for her husband, and an old man is laughing helplessly in the corner, and a little boy of perhaps eleven, who went to sleep at six, sits upright on his slab with his knees under his chin and stares at his own hands.

Wuping is there. He stands in the middle of the floor in his gray robe, turning in a slow circle, with the jade seal hanging forgotten from his hand. When he sees Jian he makes a small incoherent sound and rushes at him and seizes both his arms.

"It worked. It worked. Lu Fei says the Gate wall has stopped. They are waking."

"I see."

"You are bleeding."

"A little."

"You are bleeding a great deal." He peers into Jian's face. "Jian. What did it cost?"

Jian looks across the room. At the far end, on a raised dais under a window, a man lies on the largest slab of all. He is lean and white-haired in a green robe, his face seamed and scarred through the left brow, and his eyes are open. They are looking straight at Jian.

"A voice," says Jian. "I will tell you later."

He crosses the floor. The sleepers draw back to let him pass, whispering. He climbs the two steps of the dais and stops at the edge of the slab.

The Head looks up. His eyes are black and quite clear. He is, Jian sees, perhaps fifty years old, which is impossible; he has slept seventy. Some part of him, a fine edge of his body, was never asleep at all. He lifts one hand. The motion is slow and deliberate, and the fingers tremble like leaves.

"You are Lin Jian," he says. His voice is a rusty hinge. "The Keeper's boy."

"Yes, Master Yan."

"I was told you would come." A dry cough. "I was not told how late."

"I am sorry."

"Do not be." The ghost of a smile moves in the seamed face. "I am awake. That is a great deal more than I expected." The black eyes flick sideways, toward the window, toward the gray light and the mountain beyond. "How long?"

"Seventy years."

"Seventy." He breathes. "And the House?"

"It still stands."

"And the Gate?"

Jian hesitates. He does not like to bring this to a man so newly woken. But he has been lied to all his life by kind people, and he does not intend to add to the practice.

"It is failing. The names that fed it are gone. We have perhaps nine weeks. And the Second House will claim the stair at midwinter." He pauses. "The Warden is Shen Yuhang. He was one of ours."

"Shen." The Head closes his eyes. "Yes. I remember. A boy with a sword and a great deal of hunger." His mouth moves. "They always take the hungry ones."

"Master—"

"Help me sit."

Together, Jian and Wuping lift him. He weighs nothing. They prop him against the wall under the window, with a blanket across his knees, and he sits blinking in the gray light like an owl. Lu Fei brings a cup. He sips, and coughs, and sips again.

"Tell me," he says. "From the beginning. Do not spare me."

Jian tells him.

* * *

It takes the whole morning.

He tells it plainly, as Ye taught him: the scroll, the names, the Orchard, the tape, the Warden's ultimatum, Ye's death. He does not mention the interface. The Head does not ask. At some point a boy brings bread and tea, and Jian drinks without tasting it, and the Head listens with his eyes half shut and his hands folded on the blanket, nodding now and then, like a man hearing a story he knows the end of.

When Jian reaches the sentence from the tape, the first one was me, I built the loop, the old man's eyes open.

"Say that again."

"The first Operator. The one who built the loop. He called himself Ethan Cole."

"Cole." The Head's fingers move on the blanket. "Yes. Yes. I saw that name once. In the Founders' library, on a sheet of oiled paper, when I was young. Not in the Roll. In the margin of the Roll." His voice drops. "Someone had written it small, and scratched it out, and written it again. Cole. Cole. Cole. As though he could not make himself leave it alone."

Jian goes very still.

"You have it? The paper?"

"I have the place. Third shelf, behind the Founders' scrolls, in a box of broken lamps." The Head's dry lips twist. "I thought it a clerk's doodle. I am sorry. I would have told you, if I had known you needed it."

"You could not have known."

"No." He looks at Jian steadily. "But I know something now that I did not know when I lay down. I know what the Gate is, Keeper. Not what the House says. What it is."

"Tell me."

"It is a door that was never finished." The black eyes are very bright. "Half built. Left standing. Everything the House did, for six hundred years, was an attempt to complete it, and every attempt took something and returned nothing. The names. The sleep. The Keepers' years. And all that time, it was only waiting for the one who could finish it. The one who built it." He draws a long breath. "You do not have to feed it. You have to answer it."

"How?"

"That," says Yan Rongzhi, "I have not yet been awake long enough to learn."

He smiles. It is a thin tired smile, and Jian finds that he likes him.

* * *

The Lins arrive in the early afternoon, and they come the way they do everything, in far greater numbers than anyone asked for.

Wenyuan leads them up the ridge path in his wool mittens, with an apple-wood staff, followed by Qinghe with a basket of steamed buns on each arm and a gaggle of aunts, cousins, nephews and in-laws carrying blankets, kettles and bundles of firewood. There are forty of them at first. Then sixty. The Lin clan, the Sect's youngest and most stubborn family, has grown to five hundred and sixty souls since the Seat was granted, and it seems to Jian that at least a quarter of them have decided to help.

"We heard," says Qinghe, to nobody in particular. She marches straight to the nearest slab, where the eleven-year-old boy is still sitting with his knees under his chin, and puts a bun in his hand. "Eat. It will not bite."

The boy looks at it. He looks at her. Then, slowly, he takes a bite, and Jian sees his face change as the taste reaches him: wonder, then grief, then plain greed. He devours the bun in four swallows. Qinghe watches with her arms folded. She cannot taste anything herself, not salt, not sweet, not the ginger she grated into the filling that morning. But she has her son's sense of cooking, and she does not need a tongue to know when she has made a good thing.

"Another," she says.

Down the hall, Wenyuan has found the old man who is laughing, and is sitting beside him on the slab with one cold mitten on his shoulder, saying nothing at all. Younger Lins pass out water. A young woman of twenty-one, Lin Zhao, Yue's eldest, takes a bowl of gruel to a woman who is weeping, and holds it for her. And Yue herself stands near the door with her head tilted, listening, as she has been listening for the better part of an hour.

"Sister," Jian says.

"They hum," she says softly. She does not turn. "All of them. A little. Like the seam does." She frowns. "It is not the Gate. It is them. As if the Chain left a mark."

"Can you tell what it says?"

"No. Only that it is not finished." She looks at him then, with her mother's sharp eyes. "Jian. You have a face on you like a man who has spent his savings."

"I have."

"Was it worth it?"

He looks around the long cold hall at the waking, the weeping, the clumsy Lins with their kettles, at a child eating a bun. He lets himself feel the smooth gray space where Ye's voice used to be.

"Ask me in a year," he says.

* * *

The news arrives at dusk, with a boy of the Law benches, running.

Jian is on the dais, helping the Head drink soup, and he knows from the sound of the feet on the stair that it is bad. The boy bursts in with his queue half undone and his chest heaving, and goes straight to Wuping and speaks into his ear. Wuping's face does not change. He stands for a moment, perfectly still, like a man who has been struck on the back of the head. Then he turns.

"The Warden has fallen."

"Fallen?"

"At Lower Weir. In the Registry hall. A little before the third bell." Wuping licks his lips. "He was giving orders to his clerks. He stopped in the middle of a sentence. He put his hand to his face." A pause. "And then, they say, he began to forget. Not just a name. His name, his rank, his oath. The way to the door. Pei An reached him first. He says that the Warden looked at him and asked who he was."

Jian stares. In his mind the Roll is open, vast and white, and on its last page his own name stands in plain black ink, the thirty-second. Keeper. Beside it, where a name should be, a space has been scraped clean.

"The veil," he says. "The Warden's veil was a seat on the Roll. When I took the Keeper's place, there was no seat for him to sit."

"Is he dead?"

"I do not think so." Jian rubs his face. "I think the Roll simply stopped writing him down."

The Head, behind him, makes a small dry sound, half laugh, half cough.

"They always take the hungry ones," he says, to nobody. "And the hungry ones are always surprised."

Jian does not answer. He is looking at the window, at the gray winter light on the ridge, and a cold sense of wrongness is climbing slowly up the back of his neck. Shen Yuhang, Warden of the Roll, Golden Core, with a hundred clerks at his back, did not choose his veil. Someone gave it to him. Someone has been holding a ledger for six hundred years, and the Warden was only one line of it.

"Wuping," he says. "How many sleepers are left in the House? Not the Chain. The Second House. Their own."

"I do not know."

"Find out." He is already moving. "Because the Roll has a Keeper again. And if the Second House has a secret of its own, it knows by now that someone is reading its mail."

* * *

He goes down alone that evening, to look at the door.

It is not a thing he can do with company. He leaves Wuping and Lu Fei in the ridge-house among the waking, and walks the long way, down the seven hundred and one steps, through the Dock, past the Gate wall, to the little side passage that he has walked so often that his feet find it in the dark. At the end of it, behind a curtain of old roots, there is a plain gray door.

It is Cole's. It has always been Cole's. It is the door at which a tired man once scratched his own name on a cell wall, and it opened for Jian once, years ago, on a room full of silent pages and a smell of dust and a stranger's handwriting. Page 1 is behind it. Page 2 is behind that. Page 3, the pages of the Gate and of what he forgot, lies beyond.

He puts his hand against it. It is cold. It is, now, entirely closed.

```

Fifteen weeks, he thinks. After midwinter.

He rests his forehead against the door. It is an odd thing to do. He is sixty-three years old. He is a Keeper, a Late-stage Purple Mansion cultivator with a clan of five hundred and sixty and a Seat in the Sect of his fathers. And he stands in the dark with his head against a door that will not open, as a child does when he has been sent to bed.

"I am sorry," he says aloud. "I know I said I would come back."

The door does not answer.

From the far end of the passage, very faintly, comes a sound. Not footsteps. Something lighter. A faint dry whispering, like paper turning.

He lifts his head.

The sound is coming from the Gate wall. He goes back along the passage and out into the Dock, and the great round room is full of a soft gray light, the light of dawn on a winter field. The wall stands before him. And in the center of it, where for six hundred years there has been only blank black stone, a single line of characters has appeared.

They are small and upright and patient. They are plum-colored.

Keeper Lin Jian. The Roll thanks you for the debt.

The Second House requests an audience.

Come alone. Come before the new moon. Bring the third stone.
